A **wavetable** is a list of different single-cycle wave shapes, one after another. The oscillator
plays one shape, and a **position** control chooses which. Move the position while a note is playing
and the sound **morphs** smoothly from one shape to the next. Wolfgang Palm's PPG Wave (1981) made
the idea famous; today it's the heart of software synths like Serum and Vital.

**How to use the page.** Press **▶ Demo** or play the keys or MIDI. Drag **Position in the table**
while a note plays. The drawing shows every shape in the table, front to back, with the current one
in red.

## The synth

<div class="sk" data-w="wavetable"></div>

This table has eight shapes: sine, triangle, sawtooth, square, a narrow pulse, a vowel ("ah"), a
hollow wave and a sparse glassy one. Between two shapes the oscillator mixes them: halfway between
sawtooth and square is half of each. Look at the spectrum as you drag: each shape is a different
recipe of harmonics (see [Sound 1](sound-harmonics.qmd)), and the morph moves smoothly from one
recipe to the next.

## Scanning the table

A wavetable is most interesting when the position **moves by itself**. Raise **Scan LFO depth** and the
[LFO](sound-lfo.qmd) sweeps the position back and forth through the table. A slow scan (0.1 Hz) gives
a pad that slowly changes colour. A fast scan (4 Hz or more) gives a talking, rhythmic wobble.

In a full wavetable synth an envelope can also move the position, so that every note starts on one
shape and ends on another. That's the same idea as the filter envelope in
[subtractive synthesis](sound-subtractive.qmd), but the movement can be through any timbres at all,
not just from bright to dark.

## How it is built here

A full wavetable synth stores each shape as hundreds or thousands of samples and plays them back very
fast. For a lesson that is more than we need. The browser can build an oscillator from a list of
harmonic strengths (as in the additive widget in [Sound 1](sound-harmonics.qmd)), so each shape in this
table is stored as 48 harmonic strengths, and the position mixes neighbouring lists about thirty
times a second. Mixing harmonic recipes and mixing wave shapes give exactly the same result, so it
sounds and looks the same as the real thing, just with a smaller table.
